thread.title: Capitol Report: The uncomfortable question Zuckerberg kept facing: Is Facebook a monopoly?

title: Capitol Report: The uncomfortable question Zuckerberg kept facing: Is Facebook a monopoly?
text:
22 p.m. ET Share 
Republicans seemed to be more concerned about Facebook’s market power than Democrats Getty Images Facebook CEO Mark Zuckerberg (C) arrives at a meeting with U.S. Sen. Bill Nelson (D-FL), ranking member of the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation. 
By Francine McKenna Reporter 
Facebook sees competition everywhere, but several senators and at least one congressman think the company is a dominant monopoly with no real competitors, based on the grilling three congressional committees gave CEO Mark Zuckerberg on Tuesday and Wednesday. 
Read: Facebook’s current woes exacerbated by six-year-old FTC settlement 
Facebook FB, +0.78% told investors in its most recent annual report that its business is highly competitive and that competition “presents an ongoing threat to the success of our business.” 
Republicans seemed to be more concerned about Facebook’s market power than Democrats. The Republicans frequently fretted over examples they characterized as ways the company used its market power to limit the speech of conservative individuals, businesses and causes. 
Democrats repeatedly express concerns about the fine print of privacy disclosures, complaining it was too much to expect their constituents to read or understand before using Facebook apps and giving up their personal data. 
See also: Zuckerberg testifies before the Senate, and the internet is outraged — at senators 
On Tuesday, in a two-committee hearing that went for more then six hours, Sen. Lindsey Graham, the Republican from South Carolina, asked Zuckerberg, “Who’s your biggest competitor?” 
It was not an easy question for the Facebook CEO to answer. Facebook tells investors in its filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission that it’s not only highly focused on all of the companies it competes with every business segment, but also on the competition for capital since investors can put their money in many other rapidly growing tech companies. 
In its most recent annual report issued Feb. 1, 2018, Facebook says it is also worried about the competitive risks it faces from governments who want to sue it or impose more regulation on it and the competition for talent in Silicon Valley, in particular. The company also says it is a target for cyber attacks and other cyber misinformation campaigns like the those allegedly perpetrated by the Russian government during the 2016 election cycle that might negatively affect its reputation and erode its competitive position. 
So Zuckerberg’s answer to Graham was long but not completely satisfying to the senator. Zuckerberg identified Google GOOG, -1.12% , Apple AAPL, -0.47% , Amazon AMZN, -0.62% and Microsoft MSFT, -1.10% as tech platforms it competes with, and Twitter TWTR, -0.47% as another competitor. 
Asked by Graham if he felt Facebook had a monopoly, Zuckerberg replied, “It certainly doesn’t feel like that to me.” 
Senator Kamala Harris, the only Democrat to mention monopoly power during the hearing, noted later that Zuckerberg never really answered Graham’s question. 
“Every monopolist tries to enlarge the market definition such that his own share of it is insignificant,” said Marshall Steinbaum, the research director at the Roosevelt Institute, the nonprofit partner to the Franklin D. Roosevelt Presidential Library and Museum. “But the fact that he couldn’t name his competitors spoke volumes: Facebook controls the network over which information is proliferated, and it decides who sees what--always to its own benefit. That is a textbook monopolist and it is a company that in its current form cannot be allowed to exist.” 
Sen. Ron Johnson, a Republican from Wisconsin, noted that Zuckerberg told Graham that he didn’t think Facebook was a monopoly. “You’re obviously a big player in the space. That might be an area for competition, correct, if somebody else wants to create a social platform that allows a user to monetize their own data?” Johnson asked. Yes, says Zuckerberg. 
Sen. Dan Sullivan, a Republican from Alaska, asked Zuckerberg if Facebook was too powerful. 
“All — really all over the world, the Facebook — 2 billion users, over 200 million Americans, 40 billion in revenue. I believe you and Google have almost 75% of the digital advertising in the U.S. Is — one of the key issues here, is Facebook too powerful? Are you too powerful? And do you think you’re too powerful?” asks Sullivan. 
“Well, senator,” Zuckerberg responded, “I think most of the time when people talk about our scale, they’re referencing that we have two billion people in our community. And I think one of the big questions that we need to think through here is the vast majority of those 2 billion people are outside of the U.S. And I think that that’s something that, to your point, that Americans should be proud of. And when I brought up the Chinese Internet companies, I think that that’s a real — a real strategic and competitive threat that, in American technology policy we (inaudible) should be thinking about.” 
On Wednesday, in the hearing held by the House Energy and Commerce Committee, Rep. Fred Upton, a Republican from Michigan, noted Facebook’s potential monopoly power. “Facebook is the dominant social platform with no true competition,” Upton said, but then moved on to other questions. 
See: Facebook’s Mark Zuckerberg testifies for a second day before Congress: live blog and video 
Matt Stoller, a fellow at the Open Markets Institute who writes frequently on antitrust and completion issues, said the reason Republicans were talking more about monopoly power was that the not-for-profit think tanks Democrats turn to for talking points on technology issues are funded by those technology companies, and have been focusing on the privacy problem more than the competition issue. 
For example, the Center for Democracy and Technology says it works “to preserve the user-controlled nature of the internet and champion freedom of expression. We support laws, corporate policies, and technology tools that protect the privacy of internet users, and advocate for stronger legal controls on government surveillance.” It lists donations of more than $200,000 each from Facebook, Amazon, Apple, Google, and Microsoft and a $50,000 donation from Palantir, the data analytics firm founded by Facebook investor and board member Peter Thiel. 
Stoller told MarketWatch that legislators are “getting there” in asking Facebook the right questions about competition. “I get the sense they are starting from the perspective of consumers who might be victimized by Facebook, rather than starting from the premise of what might be a reasonable way to structure the market for citizens. It’s a learning process,” Stoller said. Related Topics
